description.narrative:
Under the Legitimate Stability Research Programme (LSRP), the Clingendael Institute, through its Conflict Research Unit (CRU) and the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) partner to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of international efforts to address present-day conflict and fragility. To do this, the LSRP provides policy and programming relevant research.
Building on a strong foundation of independent, interdisciplinary and evidence-based research, the overall objective of the LSRP is to:
Produce research outputs that can serve as relevant and timely input into the policy and programming cycles of the international community, with particular focus on the Netherlands, aiming to contribute to the development and implementation of more effective policies and programming in response to current and emerging conflict and insecurity dynamics.
Research outputs for the LSRP include research reports, policy briefs, short analytical pieces, portfolio reviews, Theory of Change reviews, scenario exercises, facilitation of workshops and trainings and the facilitation of strategy dialogues

title.narrative: Enhancing security and governance in the Horn of Africa

description.narrative: In 2022, the focus of the ISS under this project was on: Research aimed at enhancing effective responses to security and governance challenges in the Horn of Africa. Associated analysis: ISS Todays, media interviews, closed briefings and technical meetings

Many states in the greater Sahel region, such as Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, fail to deliver essential public goods and services to substantial parts of their populations. The result is that individuals often look outside of the state for their security and survival. Key here is to focus on peoples’ needs and the institutions that actually speak to these. Such a focus renders state-non-state distinctions unhelpful, and elevates the relevance of the ‘informal’
The Sahel research programme (LSRP 2022-2026) aspires to increase the understanding of how interactions between formal and informal institutions shapes governance. Our work suggests that formal and informal institutions, as well as state and non-state (armed) actors are intimately tied and that understanding ‘de facto hybridity' of governance enables policy-makers to design policies that are more attuned towards addressing fragility, conflict, and root causes of radicalisation, criminality and migration. The programme seeks to complement this ‘local’/’hybrid’ perspective with deep insight into the political economy of the central state. With this, the programme considers what hybridity means for the implementation of projects that focus on: a) supporting inclusive governance, security & rule of law, and stability; as well as, b) dealing with specific issues such as migration, organized crime and spill over. In short, we investigate which actors and institutions operate at the local and national political level, how the interactions between these actors manifest, how these actors, institutions and interactions contribute to stability (or conflict), and what consequences this has for policy measures and/or how policy measures could benefit from these insights.

title.narrative: Forward-looking analysis to enhance security and development

description.narrative: On forward-looking analysis to enhance governance, human security and development, the ISS focused on East Africa and produced four long-term forecast reports on Burundi, Kenya, Rwanda and Uganda, respectively. The ISS studies on the futures of the four East African countries used the International Futures (IFs) forecasting system with technical support from the Frederick S Pardee Center for International Futures, University of Denver, which hosts and maintains the IFs modelling platform. The ISS signed a multi-year memorandum of understanding with the African Union’s Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD) to enhance the utility of forecasting for national development planning across Africa. The agreement ensures cooperation between AUDA-NEPAD and the ISS in providing in-depth foresight analysis, scenario building, associated capacity building, and monitoring development trends for the long-term planning of the continent. Through the partnership, the ISS can work with the AUDA-NEPAD in AU member states to make available IFs expertise on long-term forecasting to national development planners and experts. During 2022 the ISS hosted expert roundtable discussions with key officials in Kenya and Uganda. Discussions on Burundi and Rwanda are scheduled for the first quarter of 2023. Each session involves sectoral experts from the government concerned and representatives from AUDA-NEPAD. The ISS also engaged the help of the Netherlands Institute of International Relations, Clingendael, and funding from SIDA and the Hanns Seidel Foundation supplemented LSRP funding for each study.

title.narrative: Thematic special project: Conflict-sensitive private sector development

description.narrative: The MFA’s Department for Sustainable Economic Development (DDE) has indicated its interest in a research component focused specifically on strengthening the knowledge base on supporting private sector development in a conflict-sensitive manner, in light of the need to increase programming on this issue in the coming years. Although the Dutch government has a range of partners and instruments available to stimulate economic recovery through DDE, many of these are not (yet) well adapted to operate in the fragile settings. Several important exceptions to this dynamic exist, showing how PSD projects can be better adapted to FCAS.1 Nonetheless, room for improvement remains for many instruments now moving into FCAS. Similarly, although conflict sensitivity guidelines have been developed, the role of economic recovery has not been sufficiently leveraged in the stabilization work of DSH. Through this research line, CRU aims to help bridge the gap between these two strands, in order to improve the appropriate integration of economic development in stabilization approaches.

The Middle East research under the LSRP examines the possibilities for political reform and renewal under authoritarian conditions. This focus is based on the realization that successive waves of protests in the Middle East against underperforming political systems, beginning with the 2011 Arab uprisings, have brought authoritarian retrenchment rather than improvement in the social contract that citizens demanded in terms of more rights and fewer duties, better publics goods/services and a higher quality of life. While making such improvements does not necessarily require a fundamental overhaul of political settlements across the region, let alone democratization, they do require improvement of the rule of law and the business climate, greater public investment as well as a reduction of the corrupt and self-regarding practices of many of the region’s ruling elites. In other words, what are the limitations and opportunities of bringing positive socio-economic change about within parameters of authoritarian rule?

title.narrative: Real time analysis and technical assistance in the Sahel and neighbouring regions along the West African coast and in the Lake Chad Basin

description.narrative:
The bulk of ISS’ engagement under the LSRP is in the Sahel, West Africa and the Lake Chad Basin, given the pressing stability, security and humanitarian issues in these regions. The ISS budgetary allocation to this work, activities detailed in the workplan and in this report therefore reflect this focus.
In 2022, the work under this project was split into three components, as follows:
1. Peace and security in the Sahel: Real-time context analysis of social, and political & human security dynamics in the Sahel, Understanding geographic and thematic grey areas, Women, peace and security in the Sahel Analytical and technical support to key policy processes and actors in the Sahel
2. Spill-over of violent extremism from the Sahel to littoral states (Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Senegal and Togo)
3. Dynamics in the Lake Chad Basin: Connecting the Sahel and the Horn of Africa

Under the thematic co-created learning budget line, CRU identifies cross-cutting topics in collaboration with key MFA stakeholders. The projects conducted under this budget line are meant to feed into learning and strengthening the knowledge base across pillars and stakeholders. In 2022, CRU used the bulk of the budget line to undertake a joint learning trajectory with the MFA on adaptive programming.

title.narrative: Horn of Africa thematic regional research

description.narrative:
With its focus on the economic interests underpinning fragility dynamics and governance arrangements, CRU’s research on the Horn of Africa has made strides in mapping, analysing and framing the political economic developments in the region. Across the states researched over the years, changes to trade patterns and funding streams within the political economy have proven to be major factors in (de)stabilisation. Such dynamics have been especially influential in the cases of Ethiopia (ethnic tensions surrounding the developmental state), Sudan (economic hardship triggering the recent revolution) and Somalia (funding of changing governance providers).
Under the LSPR, the Horn of Africa Programme continues to deepen its knowledge base on the economic factors influencing fragility dynamics by considering a range of dynamics and interests, such as individual livelihood provision, domestic constituencies, transnational interests and external financial flows. The programme explores how development and stabilisation programmes can contribute to gains in both inclusive governance arrangements of security and rule of law efforts, and inclusive economic development in fragile contexts, reducing the risks of aggravating patterns of fragility. In this way, the team supports the innovation of private sector development (PSD) approaches as well as the adaption of existing instruments to effectively support transitions to more resilient societies.
